summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for configuring and monitoring an MPLS label switching router, the device that forwards packets by looking at short labels instead of full IP addresses. It covers the router's interfaces, label mappings and cross-connects.

eli5.summary: A mail sorter reads a small sticker on each package instead of the whole address. This document defines a standard clipboard for checking how the sorter is set up.

questions: how to monitor an mpls label switching router with snmp
what is the mpls lsr mib
how to set up an lsp with snmp
subtitle: The standard SNMP data model for configuring and monitoring a label switching router: interfaces, segments, cross-connects and label stacks.

tldr.problem: Operators need a vendor-neutral way to configure and monitor the labels, interfaces and connections inside an MPLS label switching router (LSR).
tldr.mechanism: The MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB module defines SNMP tables for MPLS-capable interfaces, in-segments, out-segments, cross-connects and label stacks, plus performance tables with counters for each.
tldr.outcome: A label switched path through an LSR is set up by creating a cross-connect row and its in-segment and out-segment rows. Because the objects can change forwarding, the RFC says access must be protected, ideally with SNMPv3.

today: RFC 3813 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says the initial version of the module was published in RFC 3812 and that it works together with the shared definitions in RFC 3811.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3813 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management. Specifically, it describes managed objects to configure and monitor a Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Label Switching Router (LSR), using the MPLS architecture from RFC 3031.

MIB objects are normally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is written in SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.eli5: MPLS routers forward packets by looking at small labels. This document is a standard list of dials and gauges so any management tool can read and adjust such a router.

sections.title: Segments and Cross-Connects
sections.content:
The MIB models a label switched path (LSP) as a connection made of one or more incoming segments (in-segments) and/or one or more outgoing segments (out-segments) at an LSR. Each segment is analogous to an MPLS label.

A cross-connect is the conceptual connection between a set of in-segments and out-segments. Either set may be empty. For example, a cross-connect may have only out-segments when the LSP originates on that LSR. The terms connection and LSP are used interchangeably.
sections.eli5: A path through the router is like a pipe. The in-segment is where a package comes in, the out-segment is where it leaves, and the cross-connect is the pipe joining them.

sections.title: The Tables of the MIB Module
sections.content:
Configuring an LSP through an LSR involves enabling MPLS on capable interfaces, configuring in-segments and out-segments, setting up the cross-connect table to associate them or mark where a connection starts or ends, and optionally giving label stack actions and traffic parameters.

  • mplsInterfaceTable lists the MPLS-capable interfaces, with the label ranges in and out and the bandwidth, and the participation type (per platform, per interface or both).
  • mplsInSegmentTable and mplsOutSegmentTable describe incoming and outgoing segments. They were derived from the Incoming Label Map (ILM) and Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry (NHLFE) of RFC 3031.
  • mplsXCTable ties segments together. It supports point-to-point, point-to-multipoint and multipoint-to-point connections, with an administrative status (desired) and an operational status (actual).
  • mplsLabelStackTable gives labels to push beneath the top label.
  • mplsInSegmentMapTable maps an interface and label back to an in-segment, which helps when tracing an LSP from router to router.

Each in-segment, out-segment and interface also has a performance table that augments it.
sections.eli5: The router keeps a set of tidy tables, like a list of doors, a list of pipes and a list of who connects to whom. A manager reads or edits those lists to control the router.

sections.title: Performance Tables and Counters
sections.content:
The performance tables hold objects such as octets, packets, errors and discards per segment, and label lookup failures per interface. High capacity counters are provided for objects likely to wrap quickly on fast interfaces.

The counter rules are copied verbatim from RFC 2863. Interfaces at 20 million bits per second or less MUST support 32-bit byte and packet counters. Faster than that and slower than 650 million bits per second, they MUST support 32-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters. At 650 million bits per second or faster, they MUST support 64-bit packet and 64-bit octet counters.
sections.eli5: A fast router can count packets so quickly that a small counter rolls over, like a car odometer going back to zero. Faster links therefore need bigger counters.

sections.title: Worked Example: Setting Up an LSP
sections.content:
The RFC walks through manually creating a best-effort, unidirectional LSP that enters on MPLS interface A (ifIndex 12) and leaves on interface B (ifIndex 13), with no extra label stack beneath the top label.

First a row is created in mplsXCTable that names the in-segment and out-segment. Then a matching row is created in mplsInSegmentTable (incoming label 21 on interface 12) and in mplsOutSegmentTable (push top label 22, out interface 13). Each row is created with createAndGo(4) as its RowStatus. The RFC notes that the example leaves out some columns for brevity, and a real SET must send every column that has no default.

The traffic parameter pointers are set to zeroDotZero, which indicates best-effort treatment.
sections.eli5: To build a path, you write one line saying which door in and which door out are joined. Then you fill in a label for the way in and a new label for the way out.

sections.title: Fit with the Interfaces Group
sections.content:
This memo adds media-specific extensions to the Interfaces Group of RFC 2863. An MPLS interface is an entry in the ifTable with ifType mpls(166), stacked on any underlying layer for which MPLS interworking is defined, such as ATM, Frame Relay or Ethernet.

The RFC then gives MPLS-specific meanings for ifTable objects. For example, ifSpeed is the total bandwidth for the MPLS layer, ifPhysAddress is unused, and the octet counters count octets received or sent as labeled packets. It also explains the RowPointer textual convention. A traffic parameter pointer SHOULD point at the first accessible column of the matching resource entry in the MPLS traffic engineering MIB (RFC 3812) when the segment belongs to a TE tunnel.
sections.eli5: The MPLS part of the router shows up in the same list as all the other network ports. It simply sits on top of whatever physical port carries it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that anything configurable can be misconfigured, with potentially disastrous results. Read-write and read-create objects in the segment, cross-connect and performance tables can disrupt traffic if reached by unauthorized parties, especially once an LSP is established. SNMPv3 VACM and USM MUST be used with any v3 agent that implements this module.

Readable objects can also be sensitive, because together they reveal the LSP network topology and its performance. Versions of SNMP before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security, so the RFC says deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED and recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security enabled. Operators are responsible for giving access only to legitimate principals.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change these settings could break the network. So only trusted people should be given the clipboard, and the line to it should be locked.

data.title: Rows created for the example LSP
data.code:
mplsXCTable:
  mplsXCIndex           = 0x02
  mplsXCInSegmentIndex  = 0x00000015
  mplsXCOutSegmentIndex = 0x01
  mplsXCRowStatus       = createAndGo(4)

mplsInSegmentTable:
  mplsInSegmentIndex     = 0x00000015
  mplsInSegmentLabel     = 21
  mplsInSegmentInterface = 12

mplsOutSegmentTable:
  mplsOutSegmentIndex        = 0x01
  mplsOutSegmentInterface    = 13
  mplsOutSegmentPushTopLabel = true(1)
  mplsOutSegmentTopLabel     = 22
